definition: The DARPA AlphaDogfight was a 2019–2020 DARPA program that pitted computers using F-16 flight simulators against one another.
details: The computers were managed by eight teams of humans, who competed in a single-round elimination for the right to battle a skilled human dogfighter. Heron Systems corporation wrote a deep reinforcement learning software tool that bested the human pilot by a score of 5–0. The tournament program was managed by the Applied Physics Laboratory. The trials took place in October 2019 and January 2020 while the finals were held in August 2020. In 2024 a successor version of the program was tested with in the physical world with the X-62A.

explainer.lead: DARPA AlphaDogfight was a 2019–2020 competition in which software controlled simulated F-16 aircraft in one-on-one dogfights. It showed that a deep reinforcement learning system could defeat a skilled human pilot in the final, and a successor program later moved testing into a physical aircraft.

tiers.eli5: Imagine eight teams teaching computer players to fly pretend fighter jets, then holding a knockout contest to find the best one. The winning computer player faced an expert human pilot and won all five rounds. Later, a follow-up project tried related ideas in a real test aircraft.
tiers.practitioner: Teams built autonomous control software for F-16 flight simulators, with Heron Systems using deep reinforcement learning. The tournament provides a competitive evaluation setting, not a ready-made flight-control tool: its 5–0 result is specific to that setup and should not be treated as evidence of operational performance in real aircraft. Physical testing in 2024 involved the X-62A under a successor program.
tiers.paperLevel: AlphaDogfight can be described as a single-elimination tournament among autonomous agents A_1, …, A_8 controlling simulated F-16 aircraft, with the surviving agent evaluated against a skilled human pilot. Heron Systems' deep-reinforcement-learning agent won the final by 5–0. The result establishes performance within the competition's simulator and rules, not general air-combat capability; the 2024 X-62A tests concerned a successor version.

explainer.example: In the August 2020 final, Heron Systems' deep reinforcement learning software controlled a simulated F-16 against a skilled human dogfighter. It won five engagements and lost none, producing the 5–0 result.

parties: Applied Physics Laboratory: Managed the tournament program.
Eight human teams: Managed the competing computer systems.
Heron Systems: Developed the winning deep reinforcement learning software.
A skilled human dogfighter: Flew against the winning computer system.
explainer.outcome: Heron Systems' software emerged from the elimination tournament and beat the skilled human pilot 5–0. The competition remained simulator-based; physical-world testing came later through a successor program.
explainer.whyItMatters: The event provided a concrete demonstration of deep reinforcement learning winning a simulated air-combat contest against a skilled human. Its later successor testing with the X-62A also marks a step from simulated competition toward physical-world evaluation.
